title: Light: reflection and refraction
aim: To investigate the reflection of light by a plane mirror and the refraction of light by a rectangular glass block, by measuring the angles of reflection and refraction for different angles of incidence.
background: When light reflects from a smooth surface such as a plane mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal, which is a line drawn at right angles (90°) to the surface at the point where the ray hits it. Reflection from a smooth surface is specular (in a single direction); reflection from a rough surface is diffuse (scattered).

Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary between two materials at an angle, because its speed changes. Light slows down when it goes from air into glass, so it bends towards the normal: the angle of refraction is smaller than the angle of incidence. When it leaves the glass into air it speeds up and bends away from the normal.

A ray that hits a boundary along the normal (angle of incidence 0°) changes speed but does not change direction. For a rectangular (parallel-sided) block, the ray that comes out (the emergent ray) is parallel to the incident ray, but shifted sideways.

In this practical a ray box with a single narrow slit is used to make a thin ray of light. The paths of the rays are marked on paper with crosses, joined with a ruler, and the angles are measured with a protractor. The experiment is done in a darkened room so the rays can be seen clearly.
hypothesis: The angle of reflection will always equal the angle of incidence; for the glass block, the angle of refraction will be smaller than the angle of incidence and will increase as the angle of incidence increases.

variables.independent: Angle of incidence (°), changed in 10° steps from 0° to 70°.
variables.dependent: Angle of reflection (°) for the mirror, and angle of refraction (°) in the glass block.
control: Same glass block (same material) and same mirror
Same ray box and same narrow slit (ray width)
Same colour of light (white light or the same filter)

equipment: Ray box with a single slit, and power supply
method: Refraction: place the glass block in the middle of a sheet of plain paper and draw around it with a sharp pencil.

Remove the block. Draw a normal at right angles to one long side of the outline, near the middle, using a protractor. Mark the angles 10°, 20°, 30° and so on up to 70° from the normal with a protractor.
Replace the block on its outline. In a darkened room, shine a narrow ray of light from the ray box along the 10° line so that it hits the block where the normal meets the surface.
Mark the path of the ray leaving the opposite side of the block with two small crosses, as far apart as possible.

Remove the block. Join the crosses with a ruler to show the emergent ray, then draw a line from the point where the ray entered the block to the point where it left. This is the refracted ray inside the block.
Measure the angle of refraction between the refracted ray and the normal with a protractor. Record it.
Repeat for each angle of incidence from 0° to 70°, using a fresh sheet of paper if the lines become confusing.
Reflection: draw a straight line on a new sheet of paper and stand the plane mirror with its reflecting surface along the line. Draw a normal to the line.
Shine the ray at the mirror along lines at 10° to 70° from the normal. Mark the reflected ray with two crosses each time, join them, and measure the angle of reflection from the normal.
Repeat each measurement and calculate mean angles. Record the results in a table and compare the angle of incidence with the angles of reflection and refraction.

safety.hazard: Ray box bulb gets very hot
safety.risk: Burns to the fingers when moving or adjusting the ray box.
safety.precaution: Hold the ray box by its base or handle, do not touch the bulb housing, and allow it to cool before putting it away.

safety.risk: Tripping over bags, stools or leads.
safety.precaution: Keep bags under benches, route leads safely and keep enough light to move around safely.

safety.hazard: Glass block or mirror with sharp edges
safety.precaution: Check edges before use, handle carefully and report any damage.

results.notes: All angles are measured from the normal with a protractor to the nearest 1°, and are means of two repeats. Plot the angle of reflection against the angle of incidence (a straight line through the origin with a gradient of 1), and the angle of refraction against the angle of incidence (a curve that becomes less steep at larger angles).

analysis: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence within 1° for every ray, which supports the law of reflection. The small differences are due to the width of the ray and the resolution of the protractor.

For the glass block, the angle of refraction is always smaller than the angle of incidence (except at 0°), so the light bends towards the normal as it enters the glass. This is because light travels more slowly in glass than in air.
At 0° the ray passes straight through without changing direction, because it travels along the normal.

As the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction also increases, but not in proportion: a 10° increase from 10° to 20° increases the refraction angle by 6°, but from 60° to 70° it increases by only 4°. The ray is deviated more at larger angles (by 3° at 10°, but by 31° at 70°).

The emergent ray leaving the opposite side of the block is parallel to the incident ray, because the light bends away from the normal by the same amount on leaving as it bent towards the normal on entering.

errors.error: The ray of light is too wide, so it is hard to decide where its centre is when marking crosses.
errors.improvement: Use a narrow slit in the ray box, work in a darkened room and mark the centre of the ray.

errors.error: Crosses marked too close together, so a small error in their position gives a large error in the angle of the line.
errors.improvement: Mark crosses as far apart as possible along each ray.

errors.error: Measuring angles from the surface of the block instead of from the normal.
errors.improvement: Always draw the normal at 90° to the surface and place the protractor's centre where the ray meets the surface.

errors.error: The block moves during the experiment, so the outline and rays do not match.
errors.improvement: Draw around the block first and check it is still on its outline before marking each ray.

errors.error: Protractor resolution of 1° gives a large percentage uncertainty for small angles.
errors.improvement: Repeat each measurement, use a larger protractor and use a sharp pencil to draw thin lines.

examTips: Always measure angles from the normal, not from the surface. The normal is at 90° to the surface where the ray hits it.
Light entering a denser medium (glass) slows down and bends towards the normal; leaving it, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.
Learn the method details: narrow slit, darkened room, crosses far apart, join with a ruler, measure with a protractor.
A ray along the normal (0°) does not change direction, though it still changes speed.
For a mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. If a question gives the angle between the ray and the mirror surface, subtract it from 90° first.

questions.question: A ray of light reflects from a plane mirror. Which statement is correct?
options: The angle of reflection is always 90°
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of reflection is half the angle of incidence
The angle of reflection is always smaller than the angle of incidence
markScheme: 1 mark: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
questions.explanation: This is the law of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal.

questions.question: When measuring the angle of incidence of a ray hitting a glass block, the angle should be measured from which line?
markScheme: 1 mark: the normal
questions.explanation: All angles in reflection and refraction are measured from the normal, the line at 90° to the surface where the ray meets it.

questions.question:
A ray of light travels from air into a glass block at an angle of incidence of 40°.
Describe and explain what happens to the direction of the ray.
markScheme: 1 mark: it bends towards the normal (angle of refraction smaller than 40°)
1 mark: because light slows down when it enters glass
questions.explanation: Refraction happens because the speed of light changes at the boundary. Glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down and bends towards the normal.

questions.question:
A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the surface of the mirror is 55°.
Calculate the angle of reflection.
markScheme: 1 mark: angle of incidence = 90 − 55 = 35°
1 mark: angle of reflection = 35°
questions.explanation: Angles are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror. The angle of incidence is 35°, so the angle of reflection is also 35°. Giving 55° is a common mistake.

questions.question:
A ray of light enters a glass block with an angle of incidence of 50°. The angle of refraction is 31°.
Calculate the angle by which the ray has changed direction.
questions.explanation: The change in direction (deviation) is the difference between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction.

questions.question: Give one reason why a ray box with a narrow slit is used, in a darkened room, when investigating refraction.
acceptedAnswers: easier to mark the centre of the ray
markScheme: 1 mark: gives a thin ray / makes the ray easier to see so its path (centre) can be marked accurately
questions.explanation: A wide or faint ray makes it hard to decide exactly where to put the crosses, which leads to errors in the measured angles.

questions.question:
A ray of light enters a glass block along the normal (angle of incidence 0°).
State what happens to the direction of the ray.
markScheme: 1 mark: it does not change direction / passes straight through (it still slows down)
questions.explanation: The ray still changes speed, but because it meets the boundary at 90° it does not bend.

questions.question: A ray of light leaves a glass block and passes into air at an angle of incidence of 25°. What happens to the ray?
options: It bends away from the normal
It reflects back into the block
markScheme: 1 mark: it bends away from the normal
questions.explanation: Light speeds up as it goes from glass into air, so it bends away from the normal. The angle in air is larger than 25°.

questions.question:
When tracing a ray of light, a student marks its path with two crosses.
Explain why the crosses should be placed as far apart as possible.
acceptedAnswers: small error in position has less effect on the angle
markScheme: 1 mark: the line drawn through the crosses is more accurate
1 mark: a small error in the position of a cross gives a smaller error in the angle
questions.explanation: If the crosses are close together, a 1 mm error in one of them changes the direction of the line a lot. Far apart, the same error barely changes the angle.

questions.question:
A ray of light hits the surface of a glass block. The angle between the ray and the surface of the block is 25°.
What is the angle of incidence?
questions.explanation: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the surface. 90° − 25° = 65°.

questions.question: Which type of reflection happens when light hits a plane mirror?
options: Diffuse reflection, because the surface is rough
Specular reflection, because the surface is smooth
Diffuse reflection, because the surface is smooth
Specular reflection, because the surface is rough
markScheme: 1 mark: specular reflection, because the surface is smooth
questions.explanation: A smooth surface reflects all the light in one direction (specular). A rough surface, such as paper, scatters it in many directions (diffuse).

questions.question: Give one hazard when using a ray box in a darkened room and a precaution to reduce the risk.
markScheme: 1 mark: hazard: hot ray box / tripping in the dark
1 mark: matching precaution: do not touch the bulb housing and let it cool / keep bags and leads out of the way
questions.explanation: The filament bulb in a ray box gets very hot, and a darkened room makes it easier to trip.

questions.question:
A ray of light enters one side of a rectangular glass block with an angle of incidence of 40°. It passes through the block and leaves through the opposite, parallel side.
What is the angle between the emergent ray and the normal?
markScheme: 1 mark: 40°
questions.explanation: The ray bends towards the normal on entering and away from the normal by the same amount on leaving, because the sides are parallel. So the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray and makes 40° with the normal.

questions.question:
A student's results for a glass block show:
angle of incidence 10°, angle of refraction 7°
angle of incidence 60°, angle of refraction 35°
angle of incidence 70°, angle of refraction 39°
Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction shown by these results.
acceptedAnswers: angle of refraction increases as angle of incidence increases
markScheme: 1 mark: as the angle of incidence increases, the angle of refraction increases (and is always smaller)
1 mark: but not in direct proportion: the angle of refraction increases by less for each 10° at larger angles
questions.explanation: At 10°, the angle of refraction is 7° (0.7 of the incidence angle) but at 70° it is 39° (about 0.56 of it), so the relationship is not proportional.

questions.question: Describe a method to investigate how the angle of refraction of light in a glass block depends on the angle of incidence.
markScheme: Indicative content: place the glass block on plain paper and draw around it; draw a normal at 90° to one side using a protractor; use a ray box with a narrow slit in a darkened room; shine the ray at the block where the normal meets the surface, at a measured angle of incidence (for example 10°); mark the emergent ray with two crosses far apart; remove the block; join the crosses with a ruler and join the entry and exit points to show the refracted ray; measure the angle of refraction from the normal with a protractor; repeat for a range of angles from 0° to 70° in 10° steps; repeat and calculate means; record in a table and plot angle of refraction against angle of incidence; safety: hot ray box, tripping in the dark

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent method that would allow both angles to be measured accurately, including the normal, a narrow ray, marking and drawing the rays, measuring from the normal and a range of angles.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with the main steps (ray box, block, protractor, a range of angles) but lacking some detail, such as how the refracted ray inside the block is found.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as shine light into the block and measure the angle.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers explain how the ray inside the block is drawn (joining entry and exit points), that angles are measured from the normal, and how accuracy is improved with a narrow ray and crosses far apart.
